# SK2061 — Both operands of the operator are the same expression

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The left and right operands of a comparison, a logical operator or a subtracting, dividing or remaindering operator are the same side-effect-free expression, so the operator answers a question about nothing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S1764 |

## Why

`if (left == left)`, `a && a`, `offset - offset` — one side was meant to name something else and a copy-paste left it naming the first. The result is a constant the compiler is happy to fold, and the check that was written to catch a case cannot catch it. ⚠ **The rule must know the operand's type, which is the whole reason it is semantic.** `x == x` on a `double` is the idiomatic NaN test and is deliberate; the same text on an `int` is a bug. ⚠ **It must also know the operands cannot move.** `Next() == Next()` is two different draws written the same way, so only paths of locals, parameters and fields — never an invocation, never a property, never an index — are compared.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (candidate.start == candidate.start) { Merge(); }
```

Write:

```csharp
if (candidate.start == candidate.end) { Merge(); }

// and the NaN test, which is the same text on a different type and is never reported:
bool isNan = value != value;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Floating-point operands are excluded outright, and that exclusion is the rule.** `x == x` is how NaN is tested without calling `IsNaN`, `x != x` is the same test negated, and `x - x` is a way of producing a NaN-preserving zero; all three are deliberate and all three look exactly like the defect. `double`, `float`, `decimal` and their nullable forms therefore never reach the report, which is why the rule is `Semantic` rather than `Syntax`. ⚠ **Only side-effect-free paths of locals, parameters, fields, `this` and `base` are compared.** An invocation on either side is two evaluations that may differ — `rng.Next() == rng.Next()` and `reader.Read() - reader.Read()` are not defects — and a property access is a method call whose two reads the rule does not attempt to prove equal. ⚠ **`Math.Max(x, x)` and `a.CompareTo(a)` are invocations, not operators, and are outside the subject entirely**; a generator emitting them is not reported. ⚠ **Properties are excluded for a second reason as well**: `SK2012` already reports the automatic-property case with a proof this rule does not have, and reporting both would be one defect counted twice. A user-defined operator, a lifted (nullable-operand) operation and an operand of an unresolved type are all excluded, because none of them has the meaning the rule assumes. ⚠ **`string == string` is not one of them, and the first draft of this rule assumed it was.** It looks like a user-defined operator and Roslyn models it as a *built-in* equality with a null `OperatorMethod`, so it reaches the report — correctly: `a == a` on a string is always true and is the same copy-paste it is everywhere else. `+`, `*`, `<<` and `>>` are not examined: doubling, squaring and shifting by oneself are ordinary arithmetic. `=` is not examined either — the compiler's own `CS1717` says it, and `SK2012` says the rest. Generated code is excluded.
